item.title: 2027 Employer Health Plans: Why Open Enrollment Often Means Higher Premiums and Bigger Deductibles
item.body:
As open enrollment season begins at many workplaces, a familiar pattern is showing up in benefits packets: the cost of coverage is rising, and more of that cost is landing on employees. Surveys from benefits consultants and industry groups have pointed to continued increases in medical and prescription drug spending, and many employers say they are adjusting plan designs to manage the bill.

This guide explains why premiums and deductibles tend to climb, what to compare when you review your options for 2027, and how to avoid common mistakes before your enrollment window closes.

> **Note:** This article is for general information only. It is not medical, tax, legal, or financial advice. Plan details vary widely, so always check your own employer's official materials.

## Why Costs Keep Rising

Several forces tend to push employer plan costs up at the same time:

- **Higher medical prices and use of care.** Hospital and provider costs, along with greater use of services, can raise what a plan pays out.
- **Prescription drug spending.** Specialty medications and newer, high-cost therapies are a growing share of claims for many plans.
- **Plan renewals and insurer pricing.** Insurers and stop-loss carriers reset rates each year, and employers that self-fund their plans carry the risk of large claims directly.
- **Cost-sharing shifts.** To hold down their own spending, employers may raise employee premium contributions, deductibles, copays, or out-of-pocket maximums, or they may narrow provider networks.

The result is that a plan that looked familiar last year may cost more or work differently this year, even if the plan name has not changed.

## What Changes You May See

Not every employer makes the same moves, but common adjustments include:

1. **Higher payroll deductions.** Your per-paycheck premium may rise, and the increase is often larger for family coverage.
2. **Bigger deductibles.** You may have to pay more out of pocket before the plan starts sharing costs.
3. **Higher out-of-pocket maximums.** This is the most you could pay in a plan year for covered, in-network care.
4. **Changes to drug coverage.** Look for tier changes, new prior-authorization rules, or different copays and coinsurance.
5. **Network changes.** A doctor or hospital you use may move in or out of the network.
6. **Fewer plan choices.** Some employers consolidate options or steer people toward high-deductible plans.

## What to Compare Side by Side

Do not judge a plan by the premium alone. Build a simple comparison for each option:

| What to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Per-paycheck premium | Your guaranteed yearly cost, whether or not you use care |
| Deductible (individual and family) | What you pay before most cost-sharing begins |
| Out-of-pocket maximum | Your worst-case spending for covered in-network care |
| Copays and coinsurance | What you pay for visits, tests, and procedures |
| Prescription tiers | Whether your regular medications are covered and at what cost |
| Network | Whether your doctors, specialists, and hospital are in-network |
| Employer HSA or HRA contribution | Free money that can offset a higher deductible |

A helpful exercise: estimate your total yearly cost for each plan in two scenarios. First, a **low-use year** (routine checkups and a few prescriptions). Second, a **high-use year** (a surgery, an emergency room visit, or a new ongoing treatment). Add the annual premiums to your likely out-of-pocket costs in each case. The cheapest premium is not always the cheapest plan overall.

## Understanding High-Deductible Plans and HSAs

Many employers are expanding high-deductible health plans (HDHPs). These typically have lower premiums but higher deductibles. If you are enrolled in a qualifying HDHP, you may be eligible to contribute to a **health savings account (HSA)**.

Key HSA features to know:

- **Tax advantages.** Contributions are generally pre-tax or tax-deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Review current IRS rules for details.
- **Contribution limits.** The IRS sets annual limits that adjust over time, with higher limits for family coverage and a catch-up amount for people age 55 and older. Check the IRS figures for 2027 before you set your contribution.
- **Portability.** The money is yours and stays with you if you change jobs.
- **Employer contributions.** Some employers add money to your HSA. This can meaningfully reduce the sting of a higher deductible, so compare it carefully.
- **Eligibility limits.** Having certain other coverage, such as some general-purpose flexible spending accounts or other health coverage, can affect your eligibility. Read the plan rules.

An HDHP with an HSA can work well for people who are generally healthy and can afford to fund the account. It can be harder for people who expect frequent care and may struggle to cover a large deductible up front.

## Other Accounts and Benefits Worth a Look

- **Flexible spending accounts (FSAs).** Health FSAs let you set aside pre-tax money, but they usually have "use it or lose it" limits with specific deadlines. Check how much can be carried over.
- **Dependent care FSAs.** These can help with eligible child or adult care costs.
- **Telehealth and virtual care.** Some plans offer low-cost or free virtual visits that can reduce out-of-pocket spending for minor issues.
- **Mental health coverage.** Compare copays, visit limits, and whether therapists you use are in-network.
- **Spouse and dependent rules.** Some employers add surcharges when a spouse has access to coverage elsewhere. Look for new surcharges or eligibility changes.

## Practical Steps Before the Deadline

1. **Mark the dates.** Open enrollment windows are short, and missing one can lock you into your current choices for a year, outside of qualifying life events.
2. **Read the summary of benefits and coverage.** Employers must provide standardized summaries that make plans easier to compare.
3. **Check your doctors and prescriptions.** Use the plan's provider directory and drug list, and confirm with your providers' offices when possible.
4. **Review last year's spending.** Your past claims and explanation-of-benefits statements are a useful guide to what you may need.
5. **Look at the whole picture.** Consider premiums, deductibles, HSA or FSA options, and employer contributions together.
6. **Ask for help.** Your HR or benefits team, plan portal, or benefits hotline can answer questions about the specifics.
7. **Think about alternatives.** If you have access to a spouse's plan or are eligible for other coverage, compare it with your own employer's options. Marketplace coverage may be an option in some situations, so review eligibility rules.
8. **Confirm your choices.** Save your confirmation and review your first paycheck to make sure the deductions match what you selected.

## The Bottom Line

Rising health care and drug costs are shaping the benefits offered at many workplaces, and employees are often asked to cover more of the expense through premiums and deductibles. The best response is to compare plans on total expected cost and fit with your health needs, not just the monthly premium. Taking an hour with your benefits materials now can help you avoid surprises later in the year.

*Because plan rules, tax limits, and eligibility requirements change, verify the details with your employer, your plan administrator, and official sources such as the IRS and Healthcare.gov before making decisions.*
